claim: Fast signaling from vision and proprioception to muscle activation plays essential roles in quickly correcting movement.
source: Fast signaling from vision and proprioception to muscle activation plays essential roles in quickly correcting movement.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensorimotor control that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Many studies have demonstrated modulation of the quick sensorimotor responses as depending on context in each modality.
source: Though many studies have demonstrated modulation of the quick sensorimotor responses as depending on context in each modality, the contribution of multimodal information has not been established.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research in the field.

claim: The contribution of multimodal information to quick sensorimotor responses has not been established.
source: Though many studies have demonstrated modulation of the quick sensorimotor responses as depending on context in each modality, the contribution of multimodal information has not been established.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the existing literature that the study aims to address.

claim: A significant stretch-reflex attenuation occurs with distortion and elimination of visual-feedback without any change in motor tasks.
source: Unlike previous studies, we newly found a significant stretch-reflex attenuation by the distortion and elimination of visual-feedback without any change in motor tasks.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The stretch-reflex amplitude reduced with increasing elimination durations which would degrade state estimates.
source: Furthermore, the stretch-reflex amplitude reduced with increasing elimination durations which would degrade state estimates.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 5.

claim: Even though a distortion was introduced in the target-motor-mapping, the stretch reflex was not simultaneously attenuated with visuomotor reflex.
source: By contrast, even though a distortion was introduced in the target-motor-mapping, the stretch reflex was not simultaneously attenuated with visuomotor reflex.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 shown in Figure 8.

claim: The observed stretch-reflex attenuation is specifically ascribed to uncertainty increase in estimating hand states.
source: Our results therefore indicate that the observed stretch-reflex attenuation is specifically ascribed to uncertainty increase in estimating hand states, suggesting multimodal contributions to the generation of stretch reflexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the pattern of findings across experiments.

claim: Multimodal contributions exist in the generation of stretch reflexes.
source: Our results therefore indicate that the observed stretch-reflex attenuation is specifically ascribed to uncertainty increase in estimating hand states, suggesting multimodal contributions to the generation of stretch reflexes.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental findings showing visual effects on proprioceptive reflexes.

claim: Limb movements often deviate from planned trajectories due to imperfect learning of limb dynamics.
source: Our limb movements often deviate from planned trajectories due to imperfect learning of limb dynamics (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994), interactions between our body and the environment (Lackner and Dizio, 1994; Lacquaniti and Maioli, 1989), or the internal noise of neural processing (Apker and Buneo, 2012; van Beers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994.

claim: Limb movements often deviate from planned trajectories due to interactions between our body and the environment.
source: Our limb movements often deviate from planned trajectories due to imperfect learning of limb dynamics (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994), interactions between our body and the environment (Lackner and Dizio, 1994; Lacquaniti and Maioli, 1989), or the internal noise of neural processing (Apker and Buneo, 2012; van Beers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lackner and Dizio, 1994 and Lacquaniti and Maioli, 1989.

claim: Limb movements often deviate from planned trajectories due to the internal noise of neural processing.
source: Our limb movements often deviate from planned trajectories due to imperfect learning of limb dynamics (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994), interactions between our body and the environment (Lackner and Dizio, 1994; Lacquaniti and Maioli, 1989), or the internal noise of neural processing (Apker and Buneo, 2012; van Beers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Apker and Buneo, 2012 and van Beers et al., 2004.

claim: Feedback control mechanisms are essential to correct movements from deviations and to stabilize the motor system.
source: To correct movements from these deviations and to stabilize the motor system, feedback control mechanisms are essential.
evidence: This is a general principle in motor control supported by established knowledge.

claim: A quick implicit sensorimotor process greatly contributes to feedback control in addition to voluntary correction.
source: In addition to voluntary correction, a quick implicit sensorimotor process greatly contributes to feedback control.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the motor control field.

claim: A stretch reflex provides the function of feedback control, driven by proprioceptive input.
source: For instance, a stretch reflex provides the function of feedback control, driven by proprioceptive input.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the stretch reflex mechanism.

claim: When muscle spindles detect muscle stretch occurring with postural change, the muscle is activated quickly and involuntarily to compensate for the posture or movement error.
source: When muscle spindles detect muscle stretch occurring with postural change, the muscle is activated quickly and involuntarily to compensate for the posture or movement error, which is one of the important functions of the stretch reflex (Marsden et al., 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marsden et al., 1981.

claim: The stretch reflex occurs earlier (~30–100 ms) than the voluntary response (>~100 ms).
source: The stretch reflex occurs earlier (~30–100 ms) than the voluntary response (>~100 ms), yet it also frequently shows goal-directed modulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timing of different motor responses.

claim: The stretch reflex frequently shows goal-directed modulation.
source: The stretch reflex occurs earlier (~30–100 ms) than the voluntary response (>~100 ms), yet it also frequently shows goal-directed modulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the motor control field.

claim: Long-latency stretch reflexes (~50–100 ms) are mainly yielded via transcortical loop.
source: Long-latency stretch reflexes (~50–100 ms), which are mainly yielded via transcortical loop (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Kimura et al., 2006; Pruszynski et al., 2011), in particular exhibit flexible modulation depending on various contexts such as the instability of environments (Shemmell et al., 2009), task instructions (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Hammond et al., 1956; Shemmell et al., 2009), the direction of an up-coming external force field (Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura and Gomi, 2009), and the spatial properties of visual targets (Nashed et al., 2012; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Kimura et al., 2006; Pruszynski et al., 2011.

claim: Long-latency stretch reflexes exhibit flexible modulation depending on the instability of environments.
source: Long-latency stretch reflexes (~50–100 ms), which are mainly yielded via transcortical loop (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Kimura et al., 2006; Pruszynski et al., 2011), in particular exhibit flexible modulation depending on various contexts such as the instability of environments (Shemmell et al., 2009), task instructions (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Hammond et al., 1956; Shemmell et al., 2009), the direction of an up-coming external force field (Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura and Gomi, 2009), and the spatial properties of visual targets (Nashed et al., 2012; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shemmell et al., 2009.

claim: Long-latency stretch reflexes exhibit flexible modulation depending on task instructions.
source: Long-latency stretch reflexes (~50–100 ms), which are mainly yielded via transcortical loop (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Kimura et al., 2006; Pruszynski et al., 2011), in particular exhibit flexible modulation depending on various contexts such as the instability of environments (Shemmell et al., 2009), task instructions (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Hammond et al., 1956; Shemmell et al., 2009), the direction of an up-coming external force field (Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura and Gomi, 2009), and the spatial properties of visual targets (Nashed et al., 2012; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Hammond et al., 1956; Shemmell et al., 2009.

claim: Long-latency stretch reflexes exhibit flexible modulation depending on the direction of an up-coming external force field.
source: Long-latency stretch reflexes (~50–100 ms), which are mainly yielded via transcortical loop (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Kimura et al., 2006; Pruszynski et al., 2011), in particular exhibit flexible modulation depending on various contexts such as the instability of environments (Shemmell et al., 2009), task instructions (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Hammond et al., 1956; Shemmell et al., 2009), the direction of an up-coming external force field (Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura and Gomi, 2009), and the spatial properties of visual targets (Nashed et al., 2012; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura and Gomi, 2009.

claim: Long-latency stretch reflexes exhibit flexible modulation depending on the spatial properties of visual targets.
source: Long-latency stretch reflexes (~50–100 ms), which are mainly yielded via transcortical loop (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Kimura et al., 2006; Pruszynski et al., 2011), in particular exhibit flexible modulation depending on various contexts such as the instability of environments (Shemmell et al., 2009), task instructions (Evarts and Tanji, 1976; Hammond et al., 1956; Shemmell et al., 2009), the direction of an up-coming external force field (Kimura et al., 2006; Kimura and Gomi, 2009), and the spatial properties of visual targets (Nashed et al., 2012; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nashed et al., 2012; Pruszynski et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2011.

claim: A visuomotor reflexive response contributes to quick feedback control.
source: Additionally, a visuomotor reflexive response also contributes to quick feedback control.
evidence: This is established knowledge in motor control.

claim: Various studies have demonstrated functional modulation of quick corrective responses evoked by visual perturbations.
source: Various studies have demonstrated functional modulation of quick corrective responses evoked by visual perturbations (cursor shift or background visual motion) (Abekawa and Gomi, 2010; Franklin and Wolpert, 2008; Gomi et al., 2006; Knill et al., 2011; Saijo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Properly regulating goal-directed feedback control requires that feedback gain is adjusted with consideration to both context and current body states, including posture and motion of limb.
source: Properly regulating goal-directed feedback control requires that feedback gain is adjusted with consideration to both context and current body states, including posture and motion of limb.
evidence: This is a theoretical principle in motor control.

claim: The optimal feedback control (OFC) framework is one theory to account for the computational aspect of feedback control.
source: One theory to account for the computational aspect of feedback control is the optimal feedback control (OFC) framework (Scott, 2004; Todorov and Jordan, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scott, 2004 and Todorov and Jordan, 2002.

claim: The OFC theory proposed that our brain continuously updates state estimates of the body by combining sensory inflow and internal prediction, in order to provide a state-dependent motor command according to the control policy.
source: That theory proposed that our brain continuously updates state estimates of the body by combining sensory inflow and internal prediction, in order to provide a state-dependent motor command according to the control policy (Dimitriou et al., 2013; Izawa and Shadmehr, 2008; Liu and Todorov, 2007; Wagner and Smith, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A number of studies have suggested that the brain integrates multimodal sensory inputs in a statistically optimal manner for perception.
source: Additionally, a number of studies have suggested that the brain integrates multimodal sensory inputs in a statistically optimal manner for perception (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002) and voluntary motor control (Ronsse et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ernst and Banks, 2002 and van Beers et al., 2002.

claim: A number of studies have suggested that the brain integrates multimodal sensory inputs in a statistically optimal manner for voluntary motor control.
source: Additionally, a number of studies have suggested that the brain integrates multimodal sensory inputs in a statistically optimal manner for perception (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002) and voluntary motor control (Ronsse et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ronsse et al., 2009.

claim: For reflex control it is still under debate whether feedback responses are calculated from multisensory integration or are only generated by signals within a single modality.
source: However, for reflex control it is still under debate whether feedback responses are calculated from multisensory integration or are only generated by signals within a single modality (Cluff et al., 2015; Oostwoud Wijdenes and Medendorp, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cluff et al., 2015 and Oostwoud Wijdenes and Medendorp, 2017.

claim: Previous studies of multimodal integration predict that visual changes increase uncertainty of visual information, resulting in more weighting of proprioceptive information.
source: Previous studies of multimodal integration (Ernst and Banks, 2002; van Beers et al., 2002) predict that these visual changes increase uncertainty of visual information, resulting in more weighting of proprioceptive information.
evidence: This claim is based on predictions from cited studies on multimodal integration.

claim: If reflex gain is tuned according to sensory-weighting, an enhancement of stretch reflex could be expected when visual uncertainty increases.
source: If reflex gain is tuned according to this sensory-weighting, we could expect an enhancement of stretch reflex.
evidence: This is a hypothetical prediction based on sensory weighting theory.

claim: Visual changes will reduce the reliability of limb state estimates, due to the combination of visual and proprioceptive signals.
source: On the other hand, these visual changes will reduce the reliability of limb state estimates, due to the combination of visual and proprioceptive signals.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis based on multimodal integration theory.

claim: If reflexes are regulated according to the reliability of the multimodal state estimates, reflex gain could be reduced to suppress erroneous corrective outputs.
source: If reflexes are regulated according to the reliability of the multimodal state estimates, reflex gain could be reduced to suppress erroneous corrective outputs.
evidence: This is a hypothetical prediction based on state estimation theory.

claim: Izawa and Shadmehr (2008) have shown that the amplitude of a quick visuomotor response is reduced with increased visual uncertainty.
source: Actually, Izawa and Shadmehr (2008) have shown that the amplitude of a quick visuomotor response is reduced with increased visual uncertainty.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Izawa and Shadmehr, 2008.

claim: The finding that visuomotor response amplitude is reduced with increased visual uncertainty was limited to unimodal sensory conditions.
source: However, this finding was limited to unimodal sensory conditions.
evidence: This is an observation about the scope of previous research.

claim: It remains unknown whether visual uncertainty also affects proprioceptive reflexes.
source: It remains unknown whether visual uncertainty also affects proprioceptive reflexes.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Participants performed visually-guided wrist flexion, where they moved a cursor representing their hand position toward a visual target.
source: Participants performed visually-guided wrist flexion, where they moved a cursor representing their hand position toward a visual target (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental task as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In each experimental block, a particular angle rotation (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, or 180°) was introduced to the movement of the visual cursor.
source: In each experimental block, a particular angle rotation (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°, or 180°) was introduced to the movement of the visual cursor (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Locations of the start and the target were also rotated, so that the required hand movements (wrist flexion) were identical across the blocks.
source: Importantly, locations of the start and the target were also rotated, so that the required hand movements (wrist flexion) were identical across the blocks.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design.

claim: Variabilities of the endpoint locations of unperturbed trials significantly increased in the large angle rotations (135° and 180°).
source: Importantly, variabilities of the endpoint locations of unperturbed trials significantly increased in the large angle rotations (135° and 180°, p<0.05 by the post-hoc comparison after one-way ANOVA with p=3.65 × 10−5, F(4, 17)=7.67, partial η2 = 0.31) as shown in Figure 2B
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Averaged movement profiles (movement durations, endpoint biases, and peak velocities) of unperturbed trials did not differ significantly from baseline (0°) by adding visual rotations.
source: although averaged movement profiles (movement durations, endpoint biases, and peak velocities) of unperturbed trials did not differ significantly from baseline (0°) by adding visual rotations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A - C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Participants were correctly attending to the cursor movements, as confirmed by correctly shifted movement endpoints in the catch trials and short reaction times (198 ± 16.1 ms) to the cursor shift.
source: We also confirmed that participants were correctly attending to the cursor movements, by checking correctly shifted movement endpoints in the catch trials (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and short reaction times (198 ± 16.1 ms) to the cursor shift in the catch trials of all rotation conditions.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from catch trials.

claim: The amplitudes of the long-latency stretch reflex were significantly changed by visual rotation angle.
source: Interestingly, the amplitudes of the long-latency stretch reflex were significantly changed by visual rotation angle (one-way ANOVA, p=5.45 × 10−9, F(4, 17)=24.77, partial η2 = 0.59).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: Long-latency stretch reflexes in the greater visual rotation (≥90°) conditions were smaller than that in the baseline (0°) condition.
source: Post-hoc analyses indicated that long-latency stretch reflexes in the greater visual rotation (≥90°) conditions were smaller than that in the baseline (0°) condition (p<0.05).
evidence: This finding is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: The gain of the stretch reflex was reduced by introducing a large directional discrepancy between actual hand and visual cursor motions.
source: This means that the gain of the stretch reflex was reduced by introducing a large directional discrepancy between actual hand and visual cursor motions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The background level of EMG activity (BGA) did not differ across conditions.
source: This reduction is not explained by any changes in the background level of EMG activity (BGA in left panel of Figure 2D) which did not differ across conditions (p=0.087, F(4, 17)=2.13, partial η2 = 0.11).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data.

claim: The modulation pattern for the long-latency stretch reflex was not observed for the short-latency stretch reflex.
source: This modulation pattern for the long-latency stretch reflex was not observed for the short-latency stretch reflex (middle panel of Figure 2D), although we did find that the short latency components of 90° and 135° were significantly smaller than the baseline condition (p<0.05 by post-hoc comparison after ANOVA with p=6.07 × 10−4, F(4, 17)=5.58, partial η2 = 0.25).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The reduction of the stretch reflex amplitude more robustly occurred in the long-latency component than the short-latency one.
source: These results suggest that the reduction of the stretch reflex amplitude more robustly occurred in the long-latency component than the short-latency one.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings comparing short and long latency components.

claim: Endpoint variations significantly increased for the large angle rotations (135° and 180°) from the baseline in the Antagonist group.
source: As observed in the Agonist group, endpoint variations significantly increased for the large angle rotations (135° and 180°, p<0.05 by post-hoc comparison after ANOVA with p=1.27 × 10−4, F(4, 9)=7.78, partial η2 = 0.46) from the baseline (Figure 3B)
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Averaged movement profiles of unperturbed trials were not significantly different among visual rotation conditions in the Antagonist group.
source: while averaged movement profiles of unperturbed trials were not significantly different among visual rotation conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A - C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Significant modulation of the long-latency stretch reflex dependent on the visual rotation angles was observed in the Antagonist group.
source: As in the Agonist group, significant modulation of the long-latency stretch reflex dependent on the visual rotation angles (one-way ANOVA, p=0.011, F(4, 9)=3.83, partial η2 = 0.30) was observed (Figure 3D).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Post-hoc analysis showed significant reduction of the long-latency stretch reflex amplitude from baseline for the greater rotation angles (≥90°) in the Antagonist group.
source: Post-hoc analysis showed significant reduction of the long-latency stretch reflex amplitude from baseline for the greater rotation angles (≥90°).
evidence: This finding is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: No significant difference was found in the level of background muscle activity across the visual rotation angles in the Antagonist group.
source: We did not find a significant difference in the level of background muscle activity (p=0.68, F(4, 9)=0.572, partial η2 = 0.060), or short-latency stretch reflex amplitude (p=0.30, F(4, 9)=1.26, partial η2 = 0.12) across the visual rotation angles.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No significant difference was found in short-latency stretch reflex amplitude across the visual rotation angles in the Antagonist group.
source: We did not find a significant difference in the level of background muscle activity (p=0.68, F(4, 9)=0.572, partial η2 = 0.060), or short-latency stretch reflex amplitude (p=0.30, F(4, 9)=1.26, partial η2 = 0.12) across the visual rotation angles.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Amplitudes of the long-latency stretch reflexes decreased in both the agonist and antagonist muscles.
source: In summary, amplitudes of the long-latency stretch reflexes decreased in both the agonist and antagonist muscles, implying that distortions of visual feedback cause reductions in the gain of proprioceptive feedback, regardless of muscle acting direction.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from both the Agonist and Antagonist groups.

claim: Distortions of visual feedback cause reductions in the gain of proprioceptive feedback, regardless of muscle acting direction.
source: In summary, amplitudes of the long-latency stretch reflexes decreased in both the agonist and antagonist muscles, implying that distortions of visual feedback cause reductions in the gain of proprioceptive feedback, regardless of muscle acting direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The averaged kinematic (wrist angle) profiles of mechanically unperturbed trials did not differ largely by changing the motion direction of visual feedback, or by eliminating the visual cursor in Experiment 2.
source: The averaged kinematic (wrist angle) profiles of mechanically unperturbed trials (dashed curves in Figure 4B) did not differ largely by changing the motion direction of visual feedback, or by eliminating the visual cursor.
evidence: This is supported by kinematic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A two-way ANOVA comparing peak velocities did not find significant effect of factor for either visual feedback type or cursor visibility in Experiment 2.
source: Indeed, a two-way ANOVA comparing peak velocities did not find significant effect of factor for either visual feedback type (p=0.57, F(1, 9)=0.35, partial η2 = 0.037) or cursor visibility (p=0.68, F(1, 9)=0.18, partial η2 = 0.020).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Both mirror-reversed visual feedback and the elimination of the visual cursor increased the endpoint variability of movements in Experiment 2.
source: A two-way ANOVA with factors of visual feedback type and cursor visibility, showed that both mirror-reversed visual feedback (p=2.8 × 10−3, F(1, 9)=16.51, partial η2 = 0.64) and the elimination of the visual cursor (p=8.5 × 10−6, F(1, 9)=81.13, partial η2 = 0.90) increased the endpoint variability of movements.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction of the two effects (mirror-reversed feedback and cursor elimination) on endpoint variability was not significant in Experiment 2.
source: But the interaction of the two effects was not significant (p=0.10, F(1, 9)=3.26, partial η2 = 0.27).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of the factor of visual feedback type on the amplitude of the long-latency stretch reflex (Normal vs Mirror) in Experiment 2.
source: A two-way ANOVA showed a significant main effect of the factor of visual feedback type on the amplitude of the long-latency stretch reflex (Normal vs Mirror, p=6.0 × 10−4, F(1, 9)=26.53, partial η2 = 0.74), indicating that the long-latency stretch reflex was smaller with the mirror-reversed visual feedback than with the normal visual feedback.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The long-latency stretch reflex was smaller with the mirror-reversed visual feedback than with the normal visual feedback in Experiment 2.
source: A two-way ANOVA showed a significant main effect of the factor of visual feedback type on the amplitude of the long-latency stretch reflex (Normal vs Mirror, p=6.0 × 10−4, F(1, 9)=26.53, partial η2 = 0.74), indicating that the long-latency stretch reflex was smaller with the mirror-reversed visual feedback than with the normal visual feedback.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of cursor visibility on the amplitude of the long-latency stretch reflex (Show vs Hide) in Experiment 2.
source: There was also a significant main effect of cursor visibility on the amplitude of the long-latency stretch reflex (Show vs Hide, p=1.6 × 10−3, F(1, 9)=19.67, partial η2 = 0.69), indicating that eliminating the online visual cursor also reduced the long-latency stretch reflex gain.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Eliminating the online visual cursor reduced the long-latency stretch reflex gain in Experiment 2.
source: There was also a significant main effect of cursor visibility on the amplitude of the long-latency stretch reflex (Show vs Hide, p=1.6 × 10−3, F(1, 9)=19.67, partial η2 = 0.69), indicating that eliminating the online visual cursor also reduced the long-latency stretch reflex gain.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The ANOVA did not find significant interaction between the visual feedback type and the cursor visibility in Experiment 2.
source: As observed in the endpoint variability, the ANOVA did not find significant interaction between the visual feedback type and the cursor visibility (p=0.41, F(1, 9)=0.75, partial η2 = 0.077).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of the distorted visual feedback and the effect of the visibility of the online cursor independently contributed to the modulation of the stretch reflex gain.
source: In other words, the effect of the distorted visual feedback and the effect of the visibility of the online cursor independently contributed to the modulation of the stretch reflex gain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of interaction effect.

claim: The significant effect of cursor visibility demonstrates the contribution of visual feedback to the online tuning of the stretch reflex because the cursor was eliminated just after the movement start.
source: In particular, the significant effect of cursor visibility demonstrates the contribution of visual feedback to the online tuning of the stretch reflex because the cursor was eliminated just after the movement start.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: No significant effect of visual feedback type or cursor visibility on the level of background EMG activity was found in Experiment 2.
source: Note that, although we found small but significant differences in movement durations and endpoints among conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), probably due to the cursor elimination and mirror-reversal, we found significant effect of neither visual feedback type (p=0.61, F(1, 9)=0.27, partial η2 = 0.029) nor cursor visibility (p=0.091, F(1, 9)=3.58, partial η2 = 0.28) on the level of background EMG activity.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: No significant effects of visual manipulations on the movement speed immediately before the MP application in the perturbed trials were found in Experiment 2.
source: Nor were those visual manipulations associated with significant effects (visual feedback type, p=0.47, F(1, 9)=0.57, partial η2 = 0.060; cursor visibility, p=0.31, F(1, 9)=1.18, partial η2 = 0.12) on the movement speed immediately before the MP application in the perturbed trials.
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The observed modulation of the long-latency stretch reflex was not caused by differences in background muscle activity or by differences in movement dynamics across conditions in Experiment 2.
source: Therefore, we can exclude the possibility that the observed modulation of the long-latency stretch reflex was caused by differences in background muscle activity or by differences in movement dynamics across conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant differences in background activity and movement speed.

claim: The long-latency reflex component decreased and the endpoint variance increased in response to altered or eliminated visual feedback in Experiments 1 and 2.
source: In the above analyses of Experiments 1 and 2, we consistently observed that the long-latency reflex component decreased and that the endpoint variance increased in response to altered or eliminated visual feedback.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The negative correlation between the changes in reflex amplitude and in endpoint variance was statistically significant in the Agonist group of Experiment 1.
source: Actually, the negative correlation between the changes in reflex amplitude and in endpoint variance was statistically significant in the Agonist group of Experiment 1 (mean r = −0.46, 1000 bootstrap 95% CI [−0.62, −0.26]) and in Experiment 2 (mean r = −0.73, 1000 bootstrap 95% CI [−0.79, −0.66]).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap methods.

claim: The negative correlation between the changes in reflex amplitude and in endpoint variance was statistically significant in Experiment 2.
source: Actually, the negative correlation between the changes in reflex amplitude and in endpoint variance was statistically significant in the Agonist group of Experiment 1 (mean r = −0.46, 1000 bootstrap 95% CI [−0.62, −0.26]) and in Experiment 2 (mean r = −0.73, 1000 bootstrap 95% CI [−0.79, −0.66]).
evidence: This finding is supported by statistical analysis using bootstrap methods.

claim: The imprecision of endpoints can be ascribed to the increased uncertainty in estimating hand states.
source: Since the imprecision of endpoints can be ascribed to the increased uncertainty in estimating hand states, the stretch reflex gain reductions could be ascribed to an increase in the uncertainty of the state estimation.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking endpoint variability to state estimation uncertainty.

claim: The stretch reflex gain reductions could be ascribed to an increase in the uncertainty of the state estimation.
source: Since the imprecision of endpoints can be ascribed to the increased uncertainty in estimating hand states, the stretch reflex gain reductions could be ascribed to an increase in the uncertainty of the state estimation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Uncertainty of online state estimation gradually increases during movement for a certain duration after elimination of visual feedback.
source: Theoretically, uncertainty of online state estimation gradually increases during movement for a certain duration after elimination of visual feedback (Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wolpert et al., 1995.

claim: Actual durations of cursor elimination until the perturbations were appropriately varied among the three hide conditions in Experiment 3.
source: Although movement durations and speeds were not identical among participants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C), actual durations of cursor elimination until the perturbations were appropriately varied among the three hide conditions as shown in Figure 5B.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A significant increase in endpoint variability of the movements was found as the duration of cursor elimination became longer in Experiment 3.
